# parity-fuzz --mode trap baseline: normalized signatures of KNOWN gaps.
# A divergence whose signature is here is allowed; a NEW one fails CI.
# Regenerate: parity-fuzz --mode trap --count N --verify 3  (copy NEW-signature lines).
#
# Covers both trap spellings (`trap '…' SIG` and `TRAPSIG() { … }`, which have
# DIFFERENT semantics), EXIT/ERR/DEBUG, `always` blocks, TRY_BLOCK_ERROR,
# LOCAL_TRAPS, install-time parsing, listing, and subshell inheritance.
# Determinism: only self-sent signals (`kill -SIG $$`), no timers, no children.
#
# The mode existed but was NOT gated in CI, which is how the gaps below lived.
#
# No known gaps — 4000 cases run clean.
#
# Divergences this mode found that were real port bugs and are FIXED:
#
#   1. The trap body was not parsed at INSTALL time. C parses it in bin_trap
#      (`parse_string(arg, 1)`, c:Src/builtin.c:7405-7409) and rejects an
#      unparseable body on the spot with `couldn't parse trap command` and
#      rc=1, installing nothing. zshrs stored the text unexamined and returned
#      0, deferring the failure to delivery: `trap 'for' EXIT` reported success
#      and then emitted a parse error at exit.
#
#   2. `trap` LISTING echoed the stored text verbatim. C holds the body as
#      compiled wordcode and renders it back with getpermtext (c:7371), so the
#      listing is canonical: `trap 'print a; print b' EXIT` lists as
#      `trap -- $'print a\nprint b' EXIT`. Echoing back is right for a single
#      command and wrong for everything else — which is why the single-command
#      bodies this generator used never caught it.
#
#   3. A subshell INHERITED the parent's traps. c:Src/exec.c:1088-1092 —
#      entersubsh resets them in the child:
#          if (!(flags & ESUB_KEEPTRAP))
#              for (sig = 0; sig <= SIGCOUNT; sig++)
#                  if (!(sigtrapped[sig] & ZSIG_FUNC) &&
#                      !(isset(POSIXTRAPS) && (sigtrapped[sig] & ZSIG_IGNORED)))
#                      unsettrap(sig);
#      Not just a listing bug: an inherited trap FIRED inside the child, so
#      `trap 'print p' USR1; (kill -USR1 $$; print after)` printed p before
#      after instead of after…p — the signal is meant to reach the parent and
#      run there.
#
#      Three exemptions, and a shell that simply kept everything passes two of
#      them by accident:
#        - FUNCTION-form traps (ZSIG_FUNC) survive (c:1090).
#        - Under POSIX_TRAPS an IGNORED trap (`trap '' SIG`) survives (c:1091).
#        - The LOOP BOUND is spec, not detail: `sig <= SIGCOUNT` never reaches
#          the pseudo-signals, which zsh numbers above the real ones —
#          `#define SIGZERR (SIGCOUNT+1)`, `#define SIGDEBUG (SIGCOUNT+2)`
#          (c:Src/signals.h:34-35) — so ERR/ZERR and DEBUG traps SURVIVE a
#          subshell while SIGEXIT (sig 0) is inside the loop and is cleared.
#          Clearing the whole table looks right until `trap 'print e' ERR;
#          (trap)` stops listing the ERR trap.
#
#   4. The ERR trap fired from INSIDE a trap body:
#
#          trap 'print -r -- err' ERR; trap 'true; false' EXIT; print main
#              zsh    main
#              zshrs  main / err     <- the EXIT body's `false` re-entered ERR
#
#      C suppresses exactly EXIT, DEBUG and ZERR while another trap runs
#      (c:Src/signals.c:1112-1119):
#          if (intrap) {
#              switch (sig) {
#              case SIGEXIT: case SIGDEBUG: case SIGZERR: return;
#              }
#          }
#      with `intrap++` / `intrap--` bracketing the body (c:1123 / c:1236).
#
#      Two things were wrong and had to be fixed together — fixing either one
#      alone regresses the other:
#        - dotrapargs IS that faithful port (selective guard + intrap counter)
#          and has ZERO callers. dotrap reimplemented around it with an
#          INVENTED blanket `if (intrap) return` for EVERY signal; C's dotrap
#          (c:1244-1281) has no guard and just delegates (c:1254). The blanket
#          guard was itself a live divergence — `TRAPUSR2() { kill -USR1 $$ }`
#          runs the USR1 trap in zsh and was swallowed here. It existed as a
#          band-aid against `trap "false" ERR; false` recursing; C stops that
#          with this same guard, since ZERR is one of the three, so the
#          selective form keeps the recursion protection without swallowing
#          signals zsh delivers.
#        - The live EXIT trap runs its body through the script pipeline
#          (vm_helper.rs), not dotrap, so nothing raised intrap at all.
#          Raising it there ALONE would have regressed
#          `trap 'kill -USR1 $$' EXIT` (already correct) via the blanket guard.
#      intrap is also a COUNTER, not a flag (c:1057 `volatile int intrap`):
#      once non-suppressed signals can dispatch from inside a trap body, a
#      nested dotrap must not reset the outer one's state on the way out.
#
#      Same faithful-port-shadowed-by-a-reimplementation shape as substnamedir,
#      typeset_single and parse_string. dotrap dispatching inline rather than
#      delegating to dotrapargs is the remaining structural debt; wiring that
#      dead port back in would subsume the guard living in dotrap at all.
#
#   5. The outer EXIT trap stayed visible inside a function:
#
#          trap 'print -r -- p' EXIT; f() { trap }; f
#              zsh    (nothing)   <- EXIT is unset for the function's scope
#              zshrs  trap -- 'print -r -- p' EXIT
#
#      c:Src/signals.c:854-870 — starttrapscope, from doshfunc (c:5898):
#          if (intrap) return;            /* no special SIGEXIT inside a trap */
#          if (sigtrapped[SIGEXIT] && !exit_trap_posix) {
#              locallevel++; unsettrap(SIGEXIT); locallevel--;
#          }
#
#      starttrapscope was ported faithfully (both guards) and WAS on the live
#      path, but its `unsettrap(SIGEXIT)` reached removetrap, which cleared
#      sigtrapped[SIGEXIT] and siglists[SIGEXIT] and nothing else — while
#      zshrs's trap BODY lives in traps_table. So the unset cleared a flag the
#      live listing does not read, and the entry stayed. C frees the body right
#      there (`freeeprog(siglists[sig])`, c:843-845; c:823-830 says why: "here
#      we are remove the originals … a good deal more reliability").
#
#      Adding that removal alone is NOT enough and is worse than the bug: it
#      fixes the listing and then LOSES the trap, because endtrapscope restored
#      the saved body into traps_table BEFORE its settrap/unsettrap calls — and
#      those reach removetrap, which now deletes what was just put back. C does
#      not have this ordering hazard because it restores the body THROUGH
#      settrap (`settrap(st->sig, st->list, st->flags)`, c:925): install and
#      restore are one step. zshrs splits them (settrap(…, None, flags) plus a
#      manual traps_table insert), so the insert has to come LAST.
#
#      Both halves therefore land together:
#        - removetrap drops the traps_table body (c:843-845)
#        - endtrapscope's body restore moves AFTER its settrap/unsettrap calls
#      Reverting either one alone regresses the other — the first loses the
#      trap, the second brings the listing back.
#
#      Everything around this already behaved and must keep behaving, which is
#      what the funcscope arm checks on every case: an EXIT trap set INSIDE a
#      function fires at RETURN; POSIX_TRAPS (c:863 `!exit_trap_posix`) keeps
#      the outer one visible; inside another trap body the scoping is skipped
#      entirely (c:855-857); only EXIT is scoped (USR1/ERR are not); and the
#      LOCAL_TRAPS restore path (`trap 'o' USR1; f() { setopt local_traps;
#      trap 'i' USR1 }; f; trap`) still puts `o` back.
#
# Any divergence here is a regression.
